For sampled BCE with one positive from p(i|history) and k negatives from the actual sampler q(i|history), the unrestricted optimum is s*=log p−log q−log k (derivation; negative losses summed). Thus uniform sampling preserves p-ranking; popularity sampling q∝frequency^a subtracts a log-frequency penalty, reducing popularity shortcuts but potentially suppressing genuinely likely head items. Uniform evaluation candidates favor p-ranking, so uncorrected popularity sampling changes the target ranking. History exclusions change q’s support; unseen items can still be future positives, and popularity/hard sampling can concentrate these false negatives. Excluding observed positives cannot eliminate that uncertainty.

[gBCE, IJCAI 2024 extended abstract](https://www.ijcai.org/proceedings/2024/0939.pdf), addresses overconfidence caused by subsampling negatives, rather than arbitrary q-distribution correction. Under its uniform-negative assumptions, β=α=k/(|I|−1) recovers calibrated probabilities; practical recommendations are calibration t=0.75 and 128–256 negatives. Experiments show improvements for SASRec and sampled BERT4Rec. Calibration alone preserves ideal within-user ordering; empirical ranking gains reflect training effects, not a new Bayes-optimal ranking.

[arXiv:2410.17276](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.17276v1) evaluates SASRec on MovieLens-10M, Amazon Beauty and RetailRocket, with full-catalog ranking and 20 repeats. Uniform negatives favor head items; popularity/in-batch sampling can improve cohort balance, often sacrificing aggregate accuracy. Adaptive-mixed sampling achieves the highest overall HR@10 in all three reported datasets: uniform is not universally best. Neither paper tests NextItNet. The BCE distribution mechanism applies to its causal convolutional scores, but performance transfer remains a hypothesis. For this benchmark’s 99 uniform distractors, uniform training negatives are the directly aligned starting point; changing q requires validation, and gBCE’s scalar calibration does not remove item-dependent sampling bias.
